# Nyra

> Nyra is a small, strictly typed programming language for code that AI agents write and then run unsupervised: nearly as cheap to write as Python, native-fast, and unable to touch anything it did not declare. One `.nyra` file compiles to a native executable (through C) or to JavaScript with the `nyra` command line tool (the supported targets; Python, TypeScript, Rust and Go output also exists but is experimental). It has no semicolons, no implicit conversions, no shadowing and no null, values are copied instead of shared, and its compiler reports every error as a stable code with an exact position and a fix hint (`nyra check file.nyra --json`). A `use fs` or `use os` must be granted (`--allow fs`), or the program does not compile; `--sandbox` runs code you do not trust in an interpreter with limits on steps, memory and output. Try it in the browser at https://nyralang.dev/play/. Measured on 83 tasks: first-try pass Opus 98%, Sonnet 96%, Haiku 4.5 66% (Python 78%); about 1.2-1.3x Python's code tokens and fewer than Rust's; about 5-6 ms against about 300 ms for Python on the speed tasks (`bench/published/`).

Nyra is new and is not in your training data. It looks a little like Rust, Go and TypeScript but it is none of them: do not guess syntax, and do not use anything the docs below do not describe (files of your own are imported with `use ./name` and their `pub fn`s called `name.f(x)`; a missing value is an optional `int?`, never null; maps are `[str: int]`, `["a": 1]`, `m[k]`, `m.get(k, 0)`; the standard library is imported with `use input`, `use os`, `use fs`, `use json`, `use time`, `use random`, `use math` and `use text`, and called as `math.sqrt(x)`). Read the AI guide before you write code.

This file describes Nyra v0.7. Check the version you have with `nyra --version`: an older compiler lacks some of what is described here, and Nyra is pre-1.0, so the syntax may still change.

The ten most important rules for writing correct Nyra (v0.7):

1. A program is a script: its statements stand at the top level and run in order, so do not write `fn main()` (it is allowed, even next to top-level statements, which then run first; but it costs tokens). `fn` and `struct` definitions may appear anywhere. The script's top-level `let`/`var` variables are visible in every function, which may change the `var`s (`var pos = 0` then `fn advance() { pos += 1 }`): no need to pass them as parameters. Declare them before the first call that uses them.
2. No semicolons. One statement per line. Braces are required and `{` stays on the same line as `fn`, `if`, `else`, `while` and `for`. Comments are `// ...`.
3. Types are `int` (64-bit), `float`, `bool`, `str`, `char` (`'a'`), arrays `[T]` (`[1, 2, 3]`), optionals `T?` (`none`, `x ?? 0`, `if let v = m.get(k) { }`, `s.to_int()`), enums (`enum Dir { N, E }`, values `Dir.N`, taken apart with `match d { Dir.N => ... _ => ... }` that must cover every case; a variant may carry values: `enum Shape { Circle(float), Empty }`, `Shape.Circle(2.0)`, `Shape.Circle(r) => ...`; `match` and `if let` are values too: `let a = match s { Shape.Circle(r) => r, _ => 0.0 }`), tuples `(T, U)` (`(1, "a")`, read `t.0`, take apart `let (n, s) = t`, swap `(a, b) = (b, a)`) and structs. Parameters and return types are always written (`fn add(a: int, b: int) -> int`); local types are inferred, but an empty array needs one: `var xs: [int] = []`.
4. Types never convert implicitly: `1 + 2.0` and `"n=" + 5` are errors. Write `float(x)`, `int(x)` or `str(x)`, and write float literals with a dot (`2.0`, never `2`).
5. `let` is immutable and `var` is mutable: only a `var` can be reassigned or changed (`n += 1`, `xs.push(4)`, `p.x = 3`). A name can be declared only once while it is visible (no shadowing). Parameters are immutable unless declared `inout`, and then the call says `inout` too: `swap(inout a, inout b)`.
6. Conditions must be `bool`: `if n != 0 { }`, never `if n { }`. The boolean operators are `&&`, `||` and `!`.
7. Return with `return` (`ret` is accepted too). A function with `-> T` must end every path with `return`. A conditional value is `c ? a : b` (the same as `if c { a } else { b }`). One-line form: `fn square(x: int) -> int = x * x`.
8. `for i in 0..10 { }` counts 0 to 9 (the end is exclusive, there is no `..=`), `for x in xs { }` visits each element and `for c in s { }` each char; `while cond { }` also exists. `break` and `continue` act on the innermost loop.
9. Text: `+` joins two strings and `"sum: {a + b}"` inserts any value (a `{` or `}` that starts no value is plain text; a `$` is text too, so `"${x}"` prints `$3` and warns, E0260); a format specifier shapes it as in Python: `"{x:>8}"`, `"{n:05}"`, `"{f:.2}"`, `"{n:,}"`. Positions start at 0 and never count from the end: `xs[xs.len() - 1]`, not `xs[-1]` (E0261). `s.len()` counts characters and `s[i]` is a `char`, compared with single quotes: `s[0] == 'a'`. Chars convert explicitly: `str(c)`, `c.code()`, `char(65)`. Strings and arrays have methods (`split`, `replace`, `trim`, `upper`, `index_of`, `push`, `pop`, `sort`, `join`, `slice`, ...); there is no `len(x)`. `xs.map(x => x * 2)`, `xs.filter(x => x > 0)`, `xs.sum()` and `[x * x for x in xs if x > 0]` build values.
10. A struct is declared `struct Point { x: int, y: int }`, built with every field named in order, `Point(x: 1, y: 2)`, and has no methods, no `impl` and no `class`: write `fn area(p: Point) -> int` outside it and call `area(p)` or `p.area()`. Tuples `(1, "a")`, optionals `int?` (`x ?? 0`, `if let v = x`) and enums with `match` exist (see the spec). Assigning or passing an array or a struct copies it. `print(a, b)` prints values of any type, separated by spaces, and arrays and structs as Nyra code; a last `end: ""` replaces the newline: `print(x, end: " ")`. A failing operation (index out of bounds, integer division by zero, `int("12x")`) stops the program with a runtime error and exit code 101. An int overflow stops the program (E0255; ints never wrap), and with `--js` an int beyond 2^53 - 1 does too (E0256): for a hash, keep it small with `%` at every step.

Safety: the `use` lines are the program's permissions. `json`, `math`, `text`, `time` and `random` are always allowed; `fs` (files), `input` (stdin) and `os` (arguments, environment, `exit`) need a capability. `nyra run prog.nyra` grants all; `--allow fs,os` grants only those; `--sandbox` runs the program in an interpreter with no capability but those of `--allow`, files confined to the working folder, and limits (`--fuel`, `--max-memory`, `--max-output`, `--max-depth`, `--max-time`) that stop a runaway program with E0355 to E0359 (exit codes 120 to 124). A `use` of a module that is not granted is the compile error E0290, which names the flag to add. `nyra outline prog.nyra --json` lists the capabilities each function needs, also through its calls (`"effects"`).

Catch logic mistakes before running: after each non-trivial function write 1-2 examples with values worked out by hand, `fn sq(x: int) -> int = x * x   ex sq(3) == 9, sq(-2) == 4` (or `ex ...` on the line after a function's closing `}`). The compiler evaluates them while it compiles (they are never part of the program) and reports a false one as E0250 with the actual and expected value; `nyra test prog.nyra --json` lists them all. A property checks many inputs: `ex for n in 0..200: sq(n) >= 0` (literal range, end exclusive) reports the first failing `n` as E0250.

How to check your work: `nyra check prog.nyra --json` prints `{"ok":true,"errors":[]}` or a list of errors, each with `code`, `line`, `col`, `message` and `hint` (a `"warnings"` list, same fields, appears next to it and never fails the build). Fix them all and check again, then `nyra run prog.nyra` (add `--js` to use Node.js instead of a C compiler). `nyra run` is automatic: a program that ends within a few million steps is answered by the interpreter in milliseconds and the same program prints the same output if it runs long and goes native; `--native` always compiles first.

Let the compiler repair simple mistakes first: `nyra check prog.nyra --json --fix` applies every error that has exactly one possible repair (a `;`, `elif`, `and`, `True`, `'text'`, `xs.length()`, `string`, `Point { x: 1 }`, `5.`), checks again, and writes the file back if it then compiles (`run --fix` then runs it). Without `--fix`, `check`, `run` and `build` apply those repairs in memory and report each as a warning (`"warnings":[...]` in the JSON of `check`); `--strict` keeps errors as errors, and `nyra fmt prog.nyra` rewrites the file into canonical form. Such errors also carry the repair as `"fix":[{"line":..,"col":..,"end_line":..,"end_col":..,"text":".."}]` (replace from `line`:`col` up to, not including, `end_line`:`end_col`; columns count characters). Use `--fix` or apply the `fix` edits before asking a model to repair the program: it costs no model call. If you cannot run commands, state the output the program should print and tell the user to run `nyra run prog.nyra`.

MCP: `nyra mcp` is a Model Context Protocol server (stdio) built into the compiler; add it with `claude mcp add nyra -- nyra mcp` or `{"command":"nyra","args":["mcp"]}`. Its tools are `nyra_spec` (the agent card, about 1,400 tokens; `full: true` returns the complete spec), `nyra_check`, `nyra_test`, `nyra_run` (native or JS, or `sandbox: true` for the interpreter with limits; it grants only standard input unless `allow: ["fs", "os"]` says more), `nyra_explain` and `nyra_build`, so an agent needs no files or shell.

Editing: to change a program that exists, do not resend it. `nyra outline prog.nyra` lists its functions, structs and enums with line ranges, `nyra show prog.nyra name` prints one, and `nyra edit prog.nyra` takes new definitions on stdin (each replaces the symbol of its name) or commands (`@replace NAME`, `@add after NAME`, `@delete NAME`, `@rename NAME NEW`, `@add-field Struct name: type`, `@add-variant Enum Name(type)`). The rest of the file stays byte-identical, and an edit that adds errors is refused. The MCP tools `nyra_outline`, `nyra_show` and `nyra_edit` do the same.

## Docs

- [AI guide](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/docs/AI_GUIDE.md): read this first. The workflow, every rule as do and don't, what does not exist yet, all error codes with fixes, recipes and complete programs.
- [Agent card](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/docs/AGENT_CARD.md): the language in about 1,400 tokens: one example program, the rules that differ from other languages, what is not in Nyra, every method and module name. Put this in a prompt (and cache it) when you need the least text.
- [Language spec](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/docs/SPEC.md): the complete language: types, operators, builtins, every method of strings, chars and arrays, structs, `inout`, memory control, printing, runtime errors and known backend differences.
- [Error database](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/docs/ERRORS.md): every error code with what it means, the usual causes, and a wrong and a fixed program; `nyra explain E0201 --json` prints an entry.
- [README](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/README.md): overview, install, CLI options and roadmap.

## Examples

Every example has a matching `.out` file with the exact expected output, and runs on both backends.

- [hello.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/hello.nyra): the smallest program
- [fizzbuzz.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/fizzbuzz.nyra): `for`, `else if`, `%`
- [strings.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/strings.nyra): joining, comparing, searching, slicing and converting strings
- [chars.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/chars.nyra): `char` values, codes and character tests
- [arrays.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/arrays.nyra): every array method, nested arrays, printing
- [structs.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/structs.nyra): declaring, building, changing and comparing structs
- [inout.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/inout.nyra): functions that change the caller's variables
- [globals.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/globals.nyra): script variables used and changed by functions (a small parser)
- [loops.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/loops.nyra): `break` and `continue`
- [memory.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/memory.nyra): `free`, `arena` and `keep`
- [fib.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/fib.nyra): recursion
- [primes.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/primes.nyra): `while`, early `return`, string comparison
- [math.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/math.nyra): floats, explicit conversions, Newton's method
- [gcd.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/gcd.nyra): Euclid's algorithm, `lcm`
- [interpolation.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/interpolation.nyra): `"{expr}"` strings
- [if_value.nyra](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/examples/if_value.nyra): `if` as a value

## Optional

- [Prebuilt binaries](https://github.com/SpAkXD/nyra/releases/latest): Linux, Windows and macOS downloads of the `nyra` tool
- [Contributing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SpAkXD/nyra/main/CONTRIBUTING.md): build, test, and how to add a feature or an error code
- [Source code](https://github.com/SpAkXD/nyra): the compiler is written in Rust with no dependencies
